method: Same-agent English/Marathi close reading, equation-by-equation comparison, reverse paraphrase and structural QA. No independent human or native-speaker review is claimed.
scope: Primitive recursion from the successor structure of the natural numbers, the exponential example, recursive definitions of addition and multiplication, and the general f/g scheme.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: Every natural number is reached from zero by finitely many successor steps. Give h(0), then compute h(x+1) from h(x); iterating this defines h on every natural number.
samples.checks: The base and successor clauses, the x=0 and x=1 computations and total-domain conclusion are preserved. The frozen source's final reversed dependency is corrected under OLCMP-001.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: The equations h(0)=1 and h(x+1)=2h(x) give h(x)=2^x. Natural-number succession guarantees uniqueness. The definition is recursive because h occurs on the right and primitive because it uses only the immediately preceding value.
samples.checks: Every displayed equality and the distinction between recursive and primitive are preserved.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: For two-place functions one argument is fixed while recursion runs on the other. Addition recurs by successor. Multiplication applies addition to the preceding product and the fixed first argument; the worked 2-times-3 computation yields 6.
samples.checks: The recursion coordinate, dependence on both prior value and other arguments, and every intermediate value remain unchanged.

samples.reverse_paraphrase: In general, f gives the zero case without h and g gives the successor case from the other arguments, y and the immediately preceding h-value. Addition uses identity and successor; multiplication uses zero and addition.
samples.checks: All k-place argument lists, the order of g's arguments and the identity, constant, successor and addition specializations are preserved exactly.

source_observations: OLCMP-001 documents the frozen source's reversal of the recursive dependency in its first paragraph; the Marathi advances from h(x) to h(x+1), matching clause (b) and the later general scheme.
